p.t: In short
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t:
Aim for **at least 20 suppliers** per niche (a small product market) before you commit to it.
Launch with **two approved suppliers** and their products uploaded.

Keep **contacting new suppliers every day**, even after the store is live.
Reach **five approved suppliers** before you work on improving the store.
Keep adding brands and suppliers over time, aiming for about **20 brands**, even after the store is live.
Get **five suppliers** live on the store before you focus on making visitors buy.
If you find **too few suppliers**, widen the niche (the product group you sell) instead of launching with a small catalog.
Never depend on **one supplier**. Keep contacting new ones all the time.
Check **shipping cost** and whether the market is full of famous brands before you choose a niche.
Why the supplier count matters
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Several suppliers (companies that sell you their products) lower your business risk.
You do not depend on one vendor (seller). Brand variety also makes buyers trust you more, and it builds store credibility (the store looks trustworthy).
**Establish this foundation first**, because a stronger product base makes conversion optimization (getting more visitors to buy) work much better.
Supplier depth (how many suppliers you have) is one of the two main levers (ways to push) for growing revenue (sales money).
A dropshipping business (you sell, and the supplier ships the item to the buyer) should **secure as many suppliers as possible** within its chosen niche.
Supplier count matters because not every brand you contact will approve you (say yes to you selling its products).
You need **enough brands** that some saying no still leaves enough products on the site for the market to be viable (able to make money).
Multiple supply sources **reduce risk**, because a supplier can close, have an owner stroke (the owner becomes ill with a stroke), or move on to another project.
Expect the 80/20 pattern (about 80 percent of sales come from about 20 percent of suppliers), so **keep approaching many suppliers** and following up over time.
Set a minimum of **20 suppliers** per niche before you commit to it.
Supplier availability is checked before the product count, so you can still widen the niche (make it broader) if the count is short.

Before committing to a niche, confirm that **at least 20 suppliers** are available for it.
Before choosing a niche, identify **at least 20 potential suppliers** in your research.
Aim for **at least 20** different brands or suppliers per niche. If a niche cannot reach 20, niche up a level (broaden it) and add related products to the range.
Build a master supplier list (your full list of target brands) of **at least 20 brands** before outreach begins (before you start contacting suppliers).
Then aim to become authorized (get official permission to sell) with every viable brand on that list over the long term.
Research **at least 20 suppliers** before starting outreach, because approval rates (the share of suppliers that say yes) from day one are low for new stores.

Build a list of **at least 20 different suppliers** before you start calling. If one call goes badly, you still have 19 others to approach, so a weak first attempt does not end sourcing (finding products to sell).
During niche research, find **at least 20 different brands** you could work with. Not all will approve on day one, which is acceptable.
For the first store, find **at least 20 brands or suppliers**.
Minimum supplier count per niche (continued)
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Many will not approve, some will have low margins (little profit per sale) or no MAP (minimum advertised price, the lowest price a brand lets you show), and some may charge for access,

so the extra count is needed for a working store.
Research should yield **at least 20 suppliers**, and ideally 50 to 100 or more, to work through.
Expect about **20 suppliers** per niche as a minimum target, and as many suppliers as meet the criteria if there are more.
Plan to find **at least 20 suppliers** before launching a first store, so enough remain when many of them decline.
Find **at least 20 potential brands** per niche before launching.
Confirm they sell through online-only stores without warehouses (buildings where stock is kept), so the niche is drop-ship friendly (the brand ships straight to buyers).
Brands that sell through distributors (middlemen who stock and resell goods) with warehouses usually do not drop ship. (2023)
Require **at least 20 approved brands** and at least 100 products per store as a minimum. Expect some suppliers to reject the application, so aim for a cushion (extra room).
A store needs **at least 100 unique products** from at least 20 different suppliers. Each supplier should contribute several products rather than just one.
Aim for **at least 20 supplier candidates** (possible suppliers) early, because some rejections are expected.
That gives enough suppliers to launch, build traffic (visitors to the site) and make sales before the rest are approved.
Aim for a supplier count of **at least 20 brands** in a niche during research.
Contact **at least 20 suppliers**, because not every supplier approves a new seller on the first application. Approval standards have not become easier or harder over time.
Before testing a niche's competition, source **at least 20 suppliers**. More suppliers are always better, and 20 is the minimum for the supplier competition test. (2024)
Contact **at least 20 suppliers** to see the range of margin differences, because some will refuse and others will offer better margins. (2024)
Aim to get approved with **at least 20 suppliers** in a niche. Then put paid ad budget (money spent on paid ads) only on products from suppliers that have real margins.
A competitor site (another store selling in the same niche) listing **20 or more brands** and at least 100 products shows enough variety, even if you do not recognize the brands.
Use competitor catalogues (their product lists) to gauge this. (2023)
Working toward about **20 suppliers** on your list runs alongside the first ads, so keep the list growing while traffic runs. (2023)
Market-Specific Minimums
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Source B's market thresholds (a threshold is the minimum number that counts as enough) are lower than Source A's 20-supplier standard.

Both values apply to different situations.
**USA**
Minimum brands or suppliers: **20 or more**

When it applies: Standard US target; 20 is the threshold, 100 or more is fine
**Australia**
Minimum brands or suppliers: **More than 10** for the niche; 18 is acceptable

When it applies: Smaller market with fewer suppliers and customers, so lower competition
**UK**

Minimum brands or suppliers: **10 or more**
When it applies: Smaller market
**Any other market outside the USA**

Minimum brands or suppliers: **10 or more**
When it applies: Non-US markets generally
**Smaller countries such as the UK, Australia or Canada (Source A standard)**
Minimum brands or suppliers: **At least 20 suppliers** you can sell from before launching the niche

When it applies: Standard target; fewer is acceptable only as a temporary stage
For a US niche, **18 suppliers** would be low. The same count is acceptable for Australia.
Smaller markets have fewer suppliers and fewer customers. A lower brand threshold of **10** is accepted because competition is also lower.
Some operators (store owners) have built stores abroad with well under 20 suppliers. This carries more risk and should be treated as an exception, not a plan.
The **20-supplier target** remains the standard, even when it requires a broader niche.
Market size and warehouse-Heavy markets
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Supplier counts scale with population (the number of people).

The US, with roughly **330 to 350 million** people, has far more suppliers per niche than smaller markets. Expect to find fewer suppliers for the same product in a small country, and plan your research accordingly.
Aim for **at least 20 suppliers** that sell into the country where you do business. Finding 60 suppliers in the US is more than enough for a niche.
In markets where most suppliers keep a warehouse, expect **lower approval rates**. Contact a larger number of potential suppliers (for example **50 to 60** instead of 20) in the niche.
If too few suppliers exist, consider a broader niche to get enough products.

For a store in a country outside the US, the main constraint (limit) is usually supplier availability. Check whether enough suppliers exist locally, or whether suppliers in another country will ship into it.
US suppliers shipping into Canada is a workable option. Canadian suppliers are the ideal case because they avoid cross-border shipping (sending goods across a country border).
Build the list of potential suppliers in this order:
p.h: Building the candidate list and expected approval rates

p.t:
1. **Research and compile** a master supplier list for all potential suppliers in the niche.
2. **Complete the approval process** with the first five suppliers.
**Limit time spent on research.** Keep the list growing, but the goal at this stage is enough suppliers to launch the store.
More suppliers can be found later, sometimes when brands contact the seller after seeing it sell in their market.
**Do not spend weeks perfecting** the supplier list. At the start, you only need enough suppliers to stock the site, so you can launch and begin growing sales.

Aim for **at least 20 suppliers** in the list before moving on to the next stage. Once the store is running, more suppliers usually surface on their own, and some contact you after seeing you sell their products.

Approval rates (the share of suppliers that say yes) to plan around:
**Typical first-stage approval**

Value: **About 50 percent** at first, improving over time, with at least 20 suppliers contacted
**Decent approval including follow-ups**

Value: **50 percent** is considered decent
**New store calling suppliers**
Value: **Just over 60 percent** of suppliers called
Building the candidate list and expected approval rates (continued)
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t:
**Warning level**
Value: Approval rates **well below about 5 percent** signal a problem with the outreach method, not just bad luck
Approval is a numbers game. Expect many rejections. Write down every "reach out again" answer, and **follow up in three to six months**, sometimes a year.

Example from a bike, e-scooter and e-skateboard niche: a list of **30 brands** was built from Google Shopping listings (product results on Google search), and each brand was tracked with its phone, email
and website. The owner needed only about 10 approved suppliers for a viable start. With about 60 percent approval expected from calls, that meant roughly **19 approvals from 31 suppliers**.
A single approval is enough to start, so **calling many suppliers** is worth more than calling a few.
A new store may land **about 10 suppliers in its first week** when outreach is active. Over about six months, one partner added around 30 more suppliers for the first store.

Suppliers unfamiliar with dropshipping can take **a year or more** to approve a new seller. The first months of a store need enough runway (the time and money you have before sales arrive) to wait for approvals.
So plan the launch and budget around slow approval, rather than assuming the first application will succeed.
Approval is an ongoing process. **Keep prospecting** (searching for new suppliers) and following up while the first ads run.

Keep contacting suppliers while the store is built and running traffic. Store building and supplier outreach can run in parallel (at the same time), so **do not wait for a full supplier list** before launching.
**Do not stop supplier approvals** when ads start. Get the first two suppliers live, switch on Google ads (paid ads on Google) to create data and sales, and keep adding suppliers and products.
Apply for approval with **every brand** in the niche, including the lower-tier brands (tier means rank level), and do not stop after the first one is approved.
More approved brands give more products and more options when some are out of stock.
**Get approved with every possible supplier** in the niche. Then identify standout brands by margin strength and willingness to enforce MAP.
Approvals from **several brands**, even ones that are not the top sellers, add to store credibility. A store with more brands also makes it easier to approach larger brands in the niche later. (2023)
Aim to get approved with **every supplier** and carry every available product in the niche over time.
Launch thresholds: how many approved suppliers
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Sources differ on the launch number.

The values below apply at different stages, so each one is kept with its condition.
**Minimum to turn on paid traffic**
Value: **2 approved suppliers** with products uploaded

When it applies: Standard launch rule across sources from 2019 to 2025
**Guideline, not a hard rule**
Value: **2 approved suppliers**

When it applies: Upload all their products before ads go live
**Two to three approved**
Value: **2 to 3 approved** with products uploaded

When it applies: Activate Google Ads immediately, without waiting for all suppliers
**Four approved**
Value: **4 suppliers**

When it applies: Upload them and turn on ads; keep adding the rest in the background (2023)
**Five approved (store optimization gate)**

Value: **5 suppliers**
When it applies: Before moving to conversion rate work on the store
**Five approved (launch target)**

Value: **5 suppliers**
When it applies: Early approval target; more than five if possible
**Five active suppliers to start traffic**

Value: **5 suppliers**
When it applies: Older launch guidance; keep looking for more while ads run
**Launch with one or two**

Value: **1 to 2 approved**
When it applies: A store can launch and generate traffic and sales, but sourcing continues
**One approved for ad setup**

Value: **1 supplier**
When it applies: Enough to start setting up ads, not to turn traffic on
**Do not start traffic with one brand**

Value: **At least 2 brands** live
When it applies: Before turning traffic on
**Minimum before ads**

Value: **Products from the first supplier** uploaded, then ads start once the second supplier's products are uploaded (2025)
When it applies: Continuous addition afterward
Early on, the aim is approval from **about five silver suppliers**. Silver and gold are supplier tiers (rank levels).
Launch thresholds: how many approved suppliers (continued)
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Gold suppliers come later, after the store has built business history (a track record of sales), so do not treat them as the first target.
Your first target is to secure approval from **five suppliers**. After achieving this, continue contacting suppliers on the list to eventually build relationships with silver and gold tier suppliers.
Get approved by at least **five dropshipping suppliers** before moving on to conversion rate work, and aim for more than five if possible.
A supplier counts as complete only when its products are uploaded to the store.
Before moving on to store optimization (improving the store), have at least **five supplier approvals**. Five approved suppliers are enough to start building and optimizing the store.
The starting target is **five approved suppliers**, and the products from all five should be live in the store before moving on.
Five approved suppliers are not a finished store. The long-term target is authorization with **every brand on the master supplier list**, so keep working the list continuously.
Five approved suppliers are **only the first base**. Every additional brand can change the business, so keep working the list.
Only about **5 authorizations** are needed for the first store launch. The long-term goal is to be authorized with as close to 100 percent of the master supplier list as possible.
Approval rates are low at the start. **About five authorized suppliers** is enough to launch. The full list is worked through over time, not in one go.
Five approved suppliers are enough to start running traffic to a store. Keep looking for more suppliers while the ads are running.
Before launching a store, aim for **at least five approved suppliers**.
If you have fewer, launch only with a clear plan to keep adding suppliers and products, because a store with only two brands has limited product breadth (range of products).
**Two approved suppliers** are the minimum for sending paid traffic. A store launched on only two suppliers still needs more approvals added in the background to become a viable business. (2025)
Launch sequence with few suppliers
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Launch a new store with **at least two supplier approvals** and their products uploaded.
Then keep contacting the remaining suppliers every day, so the rest of the list does not slip to later.

Ads can start while further supplier onboarding (adding suppliers to the store) is still in progress. With two approved suppliers uploaded, running ads while the next suppliers are being added **is recommended**.
You can launch ads with just **two approved suppliers**. Upload their products, set up Merchant Center (Google's product data hub) and Google Ads, and run a small budget.
Keep recruiting more suppliers at the same time, instead of waiting for those two to produce results.
Launch Google ads with **at least two approved suppliers** uploaded, but keep working toward about 20 suppliers on the list at the same time. (2023)
Launch the store with the **first two approved suppliers** and their products uploaded. Then turn on ads, rather than waiting for all suppliers. (2025)
A store with the first two approved suppliers and their products uploaded can be launched in **about one week**. (2025)

Do not turn on paid ads until **at least two brands** have approved you and their products are live (visible to buyers) on the store. Research should identify **at least 20 possible brands** before you start applying.
Start with a small catalog (product list) of **about 20 products** from two to four approved brands before turning on ads with small budgets.
Keep applying to the remaining suppliers after the first brands are live.
**Two verified suppliers** (suppliers checked and confirmed) are enough to turn on traffic. Keep sourcing more suppliers every day, instead of waiting for sales to come in.
Do not start traffic with only one brand. Get **at least two brands** live before turning traffic on, and use the free time to get the rest of your suppliers approved.
With two verified suppliers and about **50 products**, small test budgets can be run to get the products approved and see traffic, while sourcing continues in the background.
Once the first two suppliers and their products are live, you can start ads. Keep adding more suppliers in the background at the same time. (2024)
Launch sequence with few suppliers (continued)
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Two suppliers with products uploaded are enough to start the traffic campaigns (ad runs) and remarketing (showing ads again to people who already visited the site).
**About 20 products** from two approved suppliers is enough to start.
Launch with **at least two approved suppliers**, although this is a guideline rather than a hard rule.
A store can launch with as few as **two suppliers**, with products uploaded, before starting paid traffic. Outreach for more approvals must continue daily in the background. (2024)
**Two approved suppliers** and their products (roughly 20 to 50 items) can go live with ads turned on.

Minimum product count before ads: upload products from the first supplier as soon as it is signed. Start ads once products from the **second supplier** are uploaded. Products can be added continuously afterward.
Start a new store with **two approved brands** and immediately activate Google Product Listing Ads (Google ads that show each product with its photo and price).
A launch with **20 products** from two brands is a reasonable minimum. The catalog can grow to 200 to 500 products later as more suppliers are approved.
Launch setup once the first two brands are uploaded to Shopify (online store software):
1. **Set up** the Google Product Listing Ads feed (a product data file sent to Google) and campaign.
2. **Activate** Shopify Payments (Shopify's built-in way to take card payments) so the store can accept money.
3. **Set up** Facebook dynamic remarketing (Facebook ads that show the exact products a visitor viewed).
4. **Check** that all three are working with a test. Then return to supplier approvals and keep uploading the rest of the brands.
5. Newly uploaded products are picked up automatically by the feed and remarketing, so they can start generating sales as soon as they are live.
Launch sequence with few suppliers (continued)
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Launch Shopify-style (the way Shopify stores launch) with the following sequence (2023): get the **first two suppliers** approved and uploaded, turn on Google ads, then use traffic and sales data (numbers on visitors
and sales) to choose which products to feature and which topics to cover in buyer's guides (articles that help buyers choose).

Procedure for the first live launch (2025):
1. **Get** your first two supplier approvals.
2. **Upload** those suppliers' products to your store.

3. **Remove** the demo products (placeholder sample items).
4. **Turn on** ads.
5. **Keep following up** with other suppliers in the background while traffic runs.
**All demo products must be removed** and replaced with real products from authorized suppliers before moving on to the ads step. A minimum of two suppliers is required for that step (2025).
Launch with the first few supplier approvals rather than waiting for all of them. **Once four suppliers are approved**, upload them and turn on ads.
Keep contacting and uploading the remaining suppliers in the background. (2023)
Accept having fewer products at launch, since **120 products** is enough to start. Keep adding products in the niche as suppliers approve, and make supplier outreach a daily task.

The first store can start with **about two suppliers** and their products. Go live with ads, and keep adding suppliers and products in the background every day. Do not wait to see whether the first two work.
**Start with about two suppliers** and their products, go live with ads, and keep adding suppliers in the background.
If suppliers refuse the niche at first, do not switch niches right away. Get **two suppliers**, launch the store with their products, and return to the others later, because rejections are normal.
Once a niche is chosen, **two approved suppliers** with their catalogs uploaded are enough to launch.
Launch means turning on Google Ads and Facebook remarketing to drive traffic, while approvals with more brands continue in the background.
A starting catalog of two suppliers with about five products is thin (too small). Aim for more suppliers and **roughly five to eight products** before launching ads.
**Upload all approved suppliers' products** and go live, since the store is already built.
Growing from the launch catalog
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Keep applying to more **brands** (companies that make the products you sell)
and uploading their products to your online store as each one approves you. Aim for around **20 brands** over time.
There is **no limit** on how many brands you can sell, as long as each brand approves you. Keep applying to new brands while the store is live (open to customers).
If you have few approved suppliers (companies that agree to ship orders for you), keep adding brands and products rather than stopping at launch.
Adjacent products (products close to your main ones, in the same niche) can add more brands and products. For example, ottomans or end tables next to leather chairs.
Set a goal of adding **one or two** new suppliers per week, even by going back to earlier applicants (companies that already applied).
Products from **five** different suppliers give a usable sample of items and brands to test and build on.

This is more useful than relying on a single supplier's catalog (its full product list) when choosing what to sell.
Build the first product base in this order:
1. Get **approved by five** dropshipping suppliers. (Dropshipping means you sell products, and the supplier ships them straight to the customer.)
2. Upload the products from those five suppliers to the online store.
3. Once the approvals are in and the products are live on the store, **mark this step as complete** before starting conversion work (getting more visitors to buy) on the store.

Verify that **all products** from all five suppliers are live and visible on the store before moving on.
Upload products from **each** of the five approved suppliers to the store.
Continue supplier outreach (contacting companies) and approval requests until **five suppliers** confirm they will work with the store.
Your store should have products from **at least five** different suppliers live before focusing on conversion optimization (making more visitors buy).
Once the store is running, **more suppliers** usually show up on their own.
Keep the product catalog on the store as approvals come in. Approval of a supplier alone is not enough to make progress.
Only approved suppliers with **uploaded products** add to the count needed before moving on.
Add the rest of the approved suppliers' products once the store is live. Upload **all their products before ads go live**. Ads are paid placements that show your products to shoppers.

Heavy or freight-shipped products (large items sent by truck) priced around **$1,500 to $3,000** can be a sound niche if they pass all niche criteria. Such orders can bring roughly **$500 to $1,000 profit** each. (2020)
When too few suppliers exist
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t:
If you find fewer than **20 brands** in your niche, validate viability (test whether it can work) before building.
1. **Call** companies directly.

2. Do **not** mention wanting to sell their products.
3. Ask neutrally whether they work with online distributors (businesses that sell products online).
4. Use their answers to decide whether online distribution is feasible in this niche.
To check a market with no visible dropshipping, **call the suppliers directly** and have a proper conversation about dropshipping.
Do not rely on competitor stores (other shops selling the same thing) as evidence. Supplier approval is the test that counts.
Some markets have little visible dropshipping because suppliers were not open to it in the past, while many suppliers are now more open.
Such markets can be underserved (few shops serve them) and are **worth testing**.
If a niche has only one drop-ship-friendly retailer (a shop that accepts drop shipping), check that it sells at least **20 brands** before continuing.
Then **email from a personal address** asking whether it has a warehouse (a building that stores stock) or a showroom (a space where people view products). Proceed if it is online-only. (2023)
Count how many stores advertise the most popular products of a niche on Google Shopping (Google's product search and ad page).
The competition threshold (the limit that decides pass or fail) in that test is **10 stores**. (2024)
Research the niche competition: at least **20 suppliers**, then count stores advertising the top products on Google Shopping against the threshold of **10**.
When too few suppliers exist (continued)
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Expect approval rates (the share of companies that say yes) to be low for a new store. In markets where most suppliers keep a warehouse, contact **50 to 60 suppliers** instead of 20.

If you cannot reach about **10 suppliers** after following up for roughly **two weeks**, move up one niche level (go to a wider product group) to increase the number of products you can offer at launch. (2025)
Gold-tier suppliers (the top-level, best-terms suppliers) that run out of stock: one option is to contact **more suppliers** in the niche before changing niches.
Fewer suppliers are acceptable only as a **temporary stage** in a smaller country, not as the target. (2023)
Some stores abroad are built with well under 20 suppliers, but this is an **exception**.

Estimated suppliers in a niche worksheet (a spreadsheet form where you count possible suppliers) is the count of **brands** across the future competitors you found, not the number of competitor sites.
Estimates are rough. If a brand list is long, a rounded figure such as **100** is an acceptable estimate.
The count of brands in a Google Shopping check across the product types in the niche must reach at least **10 in total**. Procedure:
1. Set the search to the target country, for example the **US** market.
2. Read the seller and brand names in the Google Shopping listings and scroll through the next pages.
3. Count the potential brands or suppliers. The rule requires at least **10 in total** across the product types in the niche.

4. Open a retailer that sells the product category and note the brands it carries.
5. Mark the local-brand criterion (one of the pass or fail rules) as **yes** if the count is met.
Broadening the Niche
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: If too few suppliers approve you, **broaden** the niche (widen it to more products) to find more brands
and products with better margins (the profit left per sale after costs). This is a fallback, not a day-one move. (2023)
If a niche cannot reach **20 suppliers**, **niche up** one level (move to a wider product group) and add related products to the range.
When niching up because you found fewer than 20 suppliers, identify an additional **20 to 40 suppliers** in related categories to expand the product range.
When a store has only a few approved suppliers with low margins or no MAP (a minimum advertised price, the lowest price a seller may show to shoppers),
grow the catalog with the steps in the section "Growing from the Launch Catalog."
In markets where most suppliers keep a warehouse and too few suppliers exist, consider a **broader niche** to get enough products.
Before choosing a niche, make sure the number of brands is **enough**. If it is short, broaden rather than launch thin (with too little).
Before moving to the niche, **confirm the supplier count first**. Supplier availability is checked before product count, so the niche can still be widened if the count is short.
Expect that some niches will have **too few suppliers** for the target count. When that happens, the broader niche is the way to reach enough products.
Supplier-count thresholds below 20 are a **temporary stage**, so widen the niche to restore the standard.
If a niche cannot reach about **10 suppliers** after **two weeks** of follow-up, move up one niche level. (2025)
Brands in a niche should be checked for drop-ship viability before broadening. A niche dominated by household names (brands everyone knows) is **not viable**, so broadening should not lead there.
Niche viability checks
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: The niche must be **drop-ship friendly**, meaning suppliers can ship orders directly to the end customer without the store holding stock.
Brands that sell through online-only stores are the ones that drop ship. Brands that sell through distributors with warehouses usually do not. (2023)
Shipping is often the **largest variable cost** (a cost that changes with each order) for heavy items. Check shipping rates before choosing a niche.
If shipping is charged out of a thin margin, such as a **35 percent** margin on a large item, the product is generally not viable, because no budget remains for ads.
The best suppliers and brands are known to enthusiasts within the market (people who follow the field closely) but unknown to the general public.
Markets dominated by household name brands are **not viable** for drop shipping.
Televisions are **not a viable** drop shipping product, because the market is dominated by massive international brands such as Sony, Panasonic and LG.
Those large companies do not need drop shippers to grow and rarely work with them.

Seasonal niches (products that sell only at certain times of the year): for a seasonal niche, for example in Texas with a short winter, start with suppliers for **year-round products** that sell in all four seasons.
Add seasonal products later, as the relevant season approaches. (2025)
Most industries see sales spikes around Black Friday, Cyber Monday (big online shopping days) and Christmas. A holiday spike alone is **not a reason to reject** a niche.
Plan around it by confirming with suppliers that stock will last through the peak.
Heavy or freight-shipped products priced around **$1,500 to $3,000** can be a sound niche if they pass all niche criteria. (2020)

Before testing a niche's competition, **source at least 20 suppliers**.
The worksheet's Estimated Suppliers number counts **brands**, not competitor sites.
Single-Supplier dependency risk
p.s: Supplier count targets and niche viability

p.t: Do **not depend on one supplier**. A single supplier can stop selling to you and remove your whole catalog.
Upload the first supplier's products and start ads, but keep contacting new suppliers continuously.
Do not start traffic (visitors to your store) with only **one brand**. Get at least **two brands** live before turning traffic on. Use the free time to get the rest of the suppliers approved.
Working with few suppliers raises business risk **sharply**. If two of three suppliers close or one raises prices, the store stays open but becomes far less profitable.
A large supplier base protects margins (profit per sale) and continuity against losing individual partners. (2023)

Multiple supply sources reduce risk. A supplier can close, have an owner suffer a stroke (a serious medical event), or move on to another project. So you need **several brands and several suppliers** in each niche.
Supplier depth (how many suppliers you have) is one of the two primary levers for growing revenue (money coming in). Secure **as many suppliers as possible** within the niche.
Put paid ad budget **only on products** from suppliers that have real margins. Send MAP suppliers' products into paid ads, and sell the rest through free traffic only.
Where a supplier enforces MAP, route its products to paid ads. Use free Google product listings (free product pages on Google) for the rest.
Set up **Google Merchant Center** (Google's tool that holds your product information) and free Google product listings for the products already approved.
Build a store with a **large supplier base** from the start. The larger the base, the less any single partner's exit can damage revenue.

Keep the master supplier list (your full list of target suppliers) continuously worked. The long-term goal is **authorization** (being approved to sell their products) with as close to **100 percent** of it as possible.
Supplier approval is a numbers game. Expect **many rejections**, and do not treat any single supplier as the business.
Expect the **80/20 pattern**: about **80 percent** of sales come from about **20 percent** of suppliers. Keep approaching many suppliers and following up with them over time.
Some operators have built stores with few suppliers, but this carries more risk and should be an **exception**.

Steps:
1. Get **approved by at least two** suppliers.

2. Upload their products to the store.
3. Enable the payment gateway (the tool that takes customer card payments).

4. Set up Google Ads (Google's paid ad system).
5. Keep submitting approvals and uploading products in the background (while you work on other things).
